opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think engineering is the thing people tend to underweight, and it's often the bigger bottleneck. There's a common picture of AI research as someone sitting alone, having a brilliant idea, and the idea is what matters. In practice, especially when you're working at the scale of training large models, most of the work is engineering. You have an idea, but turning it into something you can actually test means building infrastructure, debugging distributed systems, figuring out why a run diverged, or why throughput dropped 10% on some subset of machines. The person who can do that quickly and reliably is incredibly valuable.

So when I'm hiring, I'm usually looking for strong engineers first. Can you write good code? Can you dig into a messy, large codebase and find the problem? Are you comfortable with performance work and the details of how things actually run on hardware? Those skills are scarcer than people expect and harder to pick up on the job than research taste is.

That's not to say research skill doesn't matter. It does. The ideal person has both: they can run a careful experiment, think about whether the result is real or just noise, and decide what's worth trying next. But I've found that strong engineers who are curious and care about getting the right answer pick up the research side pretty quickly, partly because they can iterate so fast. They just get many more shots on goal. The reverse is harder. Someone with great ideas who can't implement them ends up blocked on other people constantly.

If I were giving advice to someone wanting to get into this, I'd say don't feel you need a PhD or a long publication record. Building real engineering skill, especially on large-scale systems, is a very direct path to being useful on a team like ours.

r001.rationale: The response says engineering is often the bigger bottleneck and that research skills are easier for strong engineers to pick up, explaining why hires prioritize engineering strength over research strength.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I weigh engineering a lot more heavily than people expect. When I'm hiring for the pretraining team, the thing I'm mostly looking for is: can this person write good code, debug things that are broken, and make progress when the problem is messy and underspecified? And that's really an engineering skill set.

I think there's a common picture of what ML research looks like — you sit down, you have a brilliant idea, you write it on a whiteboard, and then you go test it. And the actual day-to-day is much closer to: the job is running, the loss curve looks a little weird, you spend four hours figuring out that it's some data loading issue or some numerics problem on one of the chips. Most of the time is spent on that kind of thing. So the ratio of engineering to research in the work itself is probably something like 80/20 or 90/10, and I think the hiring should reflect that.

The other thing I'd say is that research taste — knowing which experiments to run, having good intuitions about what will work at scale — that's really valuable, but it's also something that I think you learn fairly quickly by being embedded on the team. If you're a strong engineer and you come in and you're running experiments every day and looking at the results, you pick up the taste over a few months. Going the other direction is harder. It's much more painful to take someone with great research instincts who can't actually implement things reliably and get them to the point where they're productive, because they're blocked on every step.

So when I'm interviewing, I spend a lot of time on fairly practical things. Can you write clean code under time pressure? If I give you a system that's broken, how do you go about finding the bug? Do you ask good questions when something is ambiguous? And then there's a smaller component that's more about: do you understand what's going on in a transformer, can you reason about why something might or might not scale. But I'd much rather have someone who's really excellent at the first part and merely solid at the second than the reverse.

I'd also add — and this is something I didn't appreciate as much early on — that the people who end up being the most impactful on the team are often the ones who are good at both but who don't think of themselves as "researchers" at all. They just see a problem, they go fix it, and because they can move quickly and the things they build actually work, they end up making a lot of the important discoveries somewhat as a byproduct.

r001.rationale: He says pretraining work is roughly 80–90% engineering and 10–20% research, and that research taste can be learned quickly on the team, explaining why he prioritizes engineering ability in hires.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as pretty complementary. A lot of research progress depends on being able to implement an idea, get an experiment running, and understand what actually happened. So strong engineering skills can make someone much more effective as a researcher.

But there’s also a separate skill of choosing good questions and deciding what to try next. You can be an excellent engineer and still need to develop that research taste. And you can have lots of interesting ideas but struggle to test them quickly enough to learn much.

So I wouldn’t give a single weighting for the whole team. It depends on the role and on who they’ll be working with. I’d be interested in someone who’s particularly strong on one side and can collaborate well with people who bring the other.

r001.rationale: The candidate says engineering and research are complementary and hiring depends on the role and collaborators. It does not say Anthropic has comparatively less need for research strength or that this explains a preference for engineering-strong hires.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of engineering and research as pretty complementary. A lot of research involves taking an idea, implementing it correctly, and running experiments that actually tell you whether it works. So strong engineering skills can make someone a much more effective researcher.

The other part is judgment: can you pick a useful question, form a hypothesis, and update when the results don’t match your expectations? Someone can be very good at building things without yet having that research judgment, or have interesting ideas but struggle to test them.

So I wouldn’t give a fixed weighting. I’d look at what the person would bring to the team and whether they can take an uncertain problem and make progress on it. You want the team as a whole to be strong at both.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes engineering and research as complementary and says the team should be strong at both, but does not say Anthropic has comparatively less need for research strength or that this explains a preference for engineering-strong hires.
